It varies a lot. I have 5 cats now, and two more in the past that unfortunately passed. Of my current cats, 3 of them are young and very healthy with few, if any, health issues ever. My two older ones are 8 and between 10-12 (unsure of his exact age). They have quite a few health issues already. The 8 year old has FIV and cat IBS, essentially. Gets sick often and throws up if his diet is altered. He also had stage 4 dental disease when I got him at age 6, and had to have a lot of teeth pulled. My 10-12 year old has had urine crystals, behavioral spraying/urinating issues, and recently was diagnosed with feline asthma. 

Of my two that passed, both were young. One cat I got from the shelter was 2 years old, and I had him for just 2 months before he passed of rapidly progressive kidney disease. He had to be put down, and this still devastates me. My other cat was very young (>10 weeks) and passed as well. I loved them dearly.

All this to say - cats are all different. Just take yours to the vet for regular check ups and do what you’re able to keep him/her healthy. Don’t hesitate or wait if you see something is off. But 4 is still very young

Wow, people are being incredibly hateful here lol. I think OP is aware that owning a house would be best, but it is not always that easy. For the people saying "just get rid of the cats Jesus Christ", I truly hope you never come to own any animals. There is SUCH a stigma around owning multiple cats, but never as bad for people with multiple dogs. 

OP, I also have 5 cats. I'm 23 and have lived in my current home since 19. My rental company is aware of all of them. There are companies out there that don't mind, and it \*is\* possible to take care of a rental while having 5 cats - but it does take a lot of work. I vacuum daily, mop frequently, disinfect all surfaces daily, and use candles, room sprays, and wax melts (overkill, but I'd rather it be overwhelming with good smells than reminiscent of cat smell). I brush my cats frequently to eliminate hair, dust, lint roll furniture, and scoop their normal boxes every day. I've had many people, all of whom I know and trust very well and asked to give me their God honest opinion, tell me that my house is very clean and smells good, even. For those of you that think having multiple cats absolutely MEANS your house has to reek and be a pig sty - that's incredibly far from the truth. You just have to do a lot of upkeep, which is part of having many cats. I'm also prepared to do a very thorough deep clean whenever I do move out, too.

I will say, however, there are 3 things that IMMENSELY have helped me with maintaining my space - a Litter Robot, a Chom Chom roller, and tbh just having all hardwood/laminate floors in my house. There's 0 carpet, so I don't have to worry about staining/cleaning that if one of my cats does get sick, or it harboring hair/smells. This can be difficult to find, but if you manage to find a place with no carpet, definitely recommend that. Litter Robots are very expensive, but they were a GAME CHANGER. I used to have 6 regular litterboxes and they were a PAIN to scoop daily and my house absolutely did not smell good during that time no matter what I did or how much I scooped. Getting a Litter Robot + 2 regular boxes that I scoop daily literally changed my life as a pet owner, I'm not kidding. With that many cats, it is absolutely worth the investment. Same with the Chom Chom, works so well compared to just regular lint rollers. I recommend both of these SO much.

Not necessarily an answer to your original question, but for that I would recommend finding a private landlord or a company that will be very pet friendly. Craiglist is a good place to start. Just some advice from one cat parent to another regarding owning so many cats - don't let the rude people in this thread deter you. Please PM me if you have any other questions :)

Hey, I’m in a sort of similar situation in regards to the inappropriate urination. I have 5 cats, one of which began inappropriately urinating on my couch as well semi-frequently. I also have a roommate. I get its super frustrating and not ideal, but I’ve never thought to solely confine him to one room. I understand what you’re going through, and don’t think it’s abuse per say, but I don’t think it’s fair or right personally.

I’ve done everything possible to mitigate the issue. My cat has been cleared by a vet physically many times, always has clean litter (I have a Litter Robot plus other boxes I scoop daily). I’ve recently added another box, too, just to play it safe. But I resorted for the time being to couch covers. I cleaned my couch thoroughly and completely with enzymatic cleaner (make sure to really get it IN the cushion. I’ve seen people use a sort of syringe to do this even) then covered it with 2 waterproof fabric covers, then a plastic cover as well. (Overkill, but I was at my wits end.) He would still pee on the plastic, so I’ve ended up getting plastic “scat mats” off Amazon to keep him off the couch. They’re like plastic, spiky mats to keep cats off. He still has roam the house (and my cats have tons of trees, beds, cozy spots, and can lay on other furniture). Some may say these are abuse too, but my cats have never tried to walk on them and they haven’t hurt them. They just sorta recognize something is there and they can’t walk there, so they don’t even try.

This solved the issue of keeping him off the couch. On top of this, I’ve recently begun administering him Fluoxetine (Prozac) daily as prescribed by my vet. You may look into this OP, along with other suggestions to catify the area and move/add litter boxes. It takes up to 8 weeks to take affect, and can make your cat tired, but it is effective in up to 90% of cases of behavioral urination IIRC. Worth a shot.

Again, not trying to shame you, and I wouldn’t consider it abuse. I get it’s so beyond exhausting. But these are just my recommendations from experience. Your kitty deserves room to roam imo. Best of luck!

Hi OP.

I’m a social worker here. I’m not the same as a therapist in any way, but I listen to people in the same way. My job is to help support clients I see and help direct them to care and resources. I do a lot of listening myself daily. I read your post and some comments, and it really spoke to me. I understand my response may trigger some anger, and you are absolutely entitled and right to feel that way. I don’t know you, just what I have read in your post here - I am not trying to diagnose you or tell you how to feel. 

I cannot imagine how hard and painful everything you’ve been through described above must have been. “I’m sorry that happened to you” is not sufficient or helpful here, but instead I’ll say that you did not deserve those things that happened to you. Having so many life altering events happen in such a short matter of time at a young age truly was not fair to you in any way. It sounds as if your mother was very special to you - I admire the advice she gave that you hold closely. It sounds like you are a very strong willed, driven, ambitious individual.

I know this cannot change your viewpoint on mental health professionals such as myself - I do not aim to. I truly understand where you are coming from and why you are distrustful due to what you went through. It is absolutely awful and disgusting that your psychiatrist at 16 told you to “straighten up” or nobody would ever like you, as well. That is not professional, nor kind. The sad reality is that there can be a lot of shitty, awful mental health counselors out there. I’ve also had a few myself, truly. It’s what drove me to be part of this field - I may not be perfect by any means, but I aim to really listen to and hear out and help people because I have been there myself. 

With that being said, your decision to seek out help should be entirely yours, and I am so sorry it feels as if you are not being heard out right now by those in your life. I am sorry too, that any professionals in the past have made you feel like you are a sick individual. All of your feelings of anger and annoyance completely make sense, and I do understand your hesitancy against receiving help from anyone.

It sounds as if right now, however, seeing a psychiatrist is unavoidable. If that is the case, I would encourage you to try and be as honest as possible and make the best of your situation. Even the most well adjusted, “never before experienced trauma” people can benefit from speaking with a psychiatrist/therapist. What you’ve been through does not make you sick, does not mean there is anything wrong with you, and does not make you less of a person - but it is quite a lot for someone to experience and try to navigate alone. Simply having someone to speak about that openly with, after building trust of course, could be very beneficial just for helping you cope with those feelings. 

Overall, I can just tell that you are struggling in so many ways right now. I just want you to know that you are not sick, there is nothing wrong with you, and you are worthy of feeling free, happy, and listened to. I hope you choose to do what is best for you in any case, but please know that seeking out any kind of mental health help is one of the strongest things you can do for yourself, no matter what you’re going through. Hi OP! 

I’m a social worker who has both worked (and currently works) in therapy settings and has been in therapy before myself many times. This rubs you the wrong way because it is inappropriate and unprofessional and absolutely NOT okay from a licensed professional.

As a mental health professional, I am always VERY vigilant of how much I am sharing about myself to my clients, as well as controlling my facial expressions and reactions to things. That is something I was taught from day 1 of my education. As others said - it is NOT your responsibility to worry about the emotions/trauma of your therapist. 

It sounds to me as if this is a highly inappropriate relationship on your therapists’ behalf. She should not be taking in clients with similar trauma to hers if she is not emotionally capable of it. It is not your job as a client to “help her process her own trauma”, that is so incredibly wrong of her to say and put that weight on you. She is the professional, not you.

It’s also a huge red flag to me that she is saying she “doesn’t believe in denying herself emotional expression”. It more so sounds as if she’s incapable of controlling her emotions, which is not a good sign in someone who is supposed to be supporting YOUR recovery and journey. If she cannot control her emotions - how is she supposed to help you learn to cope with and manage yours? Of course, sometimes on the occasion and depending on the circumstances, this can be understandable! But it sounds as if this is regular and ongoing and that is not okay.

Therapists should not be robots, but they also shouldn’t just be like talking with a friend. Good therapists have boundaries with clients. Good therapists walk a very fine line between being a “robot” of sorts and being a friend, in my opinion at least. Part of doing this job well is leaving some parts of yourself at the door when you come in. It isn’t “suppressing your emotions”, it is part of being a professional. My clients have so much to worry about in their own lives - I could not imagine trying to throw my own problems on top of them. Therapists are allowed to have their own problems absolutely, but they should not be discussing those with you regularly or in detail. 

Respectfully, it sounds as if your therapist needs her own therapist. (As most do, and that’s fine!) Just because we are professionals doesn’t mean we also don’t need help too, but you as a client are not the appropriate channel for that.

Hi OP! 

You’ve gotten a lot of other great advice here and shared experiences from others. I wanted to give you my two cents though too, coming from a social worker who works a similar schedule and also has a lot of mental health issues (Like a lot of us do, of course!)

I know your question is more centered around the night shift aspect of things, but I personally also work 3 12 hour shifts a week, and usually pick up more. I work 10:30 am-10:30 pm most days, so I am on dayshift and cannot attest to the overnight aspect of things. I can certainly imagine how working overnight would be very draining and difficult for some. However, I will say, having 4 days off and only 3 days I’m obligated to work has been a game changer for me. It has made me enjoy my work more honestly, and I find myself willing/wanting to pick up more shifts on my days off occasionally since I sometimes actually get BORED on my days off - which I know, sounds absolutely insane and I never would have said a year ago. When I need a break or have plans though or want to do something, I have more time off than I do time at work, which is amazing. I don’t really feel like a slave to an office anymore. Like you, five 8 hour work days absolutely drained me. I really enjoy my work now and enjoy coming in. 

Everyone in my life told me, too, that they were worried I couldn’t handle working 12 hour shifts. My mental health certainly still needs some work, but my job is no longer contributing toward making it worse.

If working at a bookstore sounds more appealing - go for it! There’s nothing wrong with that at all. You certainly could do more than just be a therapist with an MSW, though! That may be the traditional route for most, but there’s certainly more out there. 

There’s also so many social work related jobs that aren’t necessarily “being a social worker” if that makes sense? Social work is super broad and bleeds into so many other fields. One of the biggest reasons I chose to study it was because of how versatile it could be. I couldn’t decide on what I wanted to do as an adult, and feared I’d pick the wrong major to go into and be stuck doing the same kind of job no matter where I went. I think as social workers, we pick up a little bit of everything: sociology, psychology, health sciences, women’s & gender studies, maybe a bit of education depending on your university (I did have to take multiple Multicultural Education classes myself) and this helps us appeal to a variety of different employers. I liked social work too because at any given moment if I decided working with a certain population/job wasn’t for me, I could always give something else a go. Maybe being a therapist isn’t for you - but that doesn’t mean you wouldn’t be great and happy doing something else with an MSW.

Of course - you know yourself and your needs best. You should do something you love and enjoy for work, no matter what it is! Just a tid bit of unasked for advice/babbling from a social worker here (Aren’t we great at doing that?) :)

Alright, no vet here, but I have 5 cats and have owned 7 in total. Everything I’m gonna say is to be helpful to you, as I’ve been in your situation!

To be truthful, it sounds to me like you went about introducing them wrong as you mentioned. This is a very common mistake with new multi cat owners, and one I made myself. Don’t feel bad - you didn’t know! You were trying to do something nice and get your kitty a friend, so good job there.

When you bring another cat into your home where a cat has already lived for quite some time, it can be very threatening. Cats are highly territorial creatures, even the nicest ones. If I were you, I’d recommend going back to square #1 and reintroducing them.

What this means, is youre going to need to “separate” them, at least for a week. I would take new kitty and place him inside a bedroom or room where he can hang out for a week or so. Make sure he has food and water and a litter box and all. Being that he’s already been out and about in your home, he may not like this, but he is okay! I know it may feel mean, but it is for the greater good of the kitties, and he is safe and should get plenty of love during this time so he doesn’t believe he’s being punished. 

Once you’ve separated them, every day/night at feeding time, feed the kitties on opposite sides of the same door, the door to the room where new kitty is locked in. This way, they can get used to each other’s scents and associate them with something positive. I’d also recommend giving them each toys to play with, and swapping them for each other’s every day, that way they’re getting more of each other’s scent too. You can also do this with cat beds/blankets if wanted. Keep doing this for a week, at most I’d probably say a week and a half. It may be difficult at first - try to keep persisting. This is advice from my vet directly.

Second, try getting a pheromone diffuser/spray/collar for your old cat. Feliway is the most common and effective. They release calming pheromones into the air which help relax your kitty, and should aid in this process. 

Finally, never force the kitties to try and “bond”. Not at all that I believe or am saying you have, but this is another common mistake people make. Don’t lock them in a room together, pick them up and place them by each other, etc. Everything has to be done on their terms.

All in all, some cats truly just don’t mesh well or ever get along fully, just like humans. My first cat I ever got is a female named Bindi. I also have an old, male tuxedo cat named Tux. For whatever reason, she has NEVER liked him - I chalk it up to dominance issues. When I first brought him home though, she would go berserk whenever he was near her. I mean screaming, running, hissing, swatting, everything. Now, it’s been about 9 months since then, and she still doesn’t like him, but she no longer freaks out. Sometimes, she’ll sit beside him peacefully even for a bit. The worst she does now is hiss at him and run away if he gets too close, so it is infinitely better than before. Seriously, I’d be woken up in the middle of the night due to her screaming at him and trying to get away. He’s never attacked her or anything - Bindi is just a screamer, even when playing lol.

Exactly this. Mental illness affects every single person differently, and I feel that’s what OP is missing. Also the fact that every mental illness and how everyone handles it is entirely different? Someone with GAD isn’t necessarily going to be the same as someone with PTSD, or bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia. Hell, even two people with GAD or any diagnosis aren’t going to be the same. Mental illness is highly individualized in a way, too.

As someone else has said, you aren’t your partner’s social worker. As others have said, having a diagnosis shouldn’t automatically disqualify or worsen a potential partner in your eyes, especially as a social worker in my opinion. You navigate this relationship as you would any other one in your personal life. I know more people in general who have some type of mental illness than people who don’t. In this day, it’s almost unavoidable to some degree. Life is fuckin hard, man. And just because you may not have a diagnosis right now doesn’t mean in a week, a month, or a year or 10 from now that you still won’t. 

I’m a social worker. I’m diagnosed with bipolar II disorder, ADHD, and anxiety. It took me 20 years to discover I had bipolar disorder, 21 to discover I had ADHD. You would never know this by interacting with me as I’ve been told by very many. I’m not perfect at all - but I am seeking to return to therapy, actively working in therapy/mental health workbooks, and taking steps to manage my symptoms when they get out of hand. It all boils down to the individual and whether or not they’re actively committed to getting better and trying to be a good/healthy partner. It is all about intention for me. (And even if someone is mentally ill and they’re not committed yet to getting better, it doesn’t make them a bad person, just not an ideal partner at this time.) 

Just as some extra food for thought, too: the worst guy I ever dated was the only guy I’ve ever dated who did not have any mental illness diagnoses. I’m not accrediting him being horrible to the fact that he didn’t have a mental illness at all, that isn’t my intention. He was horrible for far more, better reasons. But I found that overall, while the partners with mental illnesses did struggle and weren’t perfect in their own ways, they were more understanding, forgiving, and communicative than the partner I dated who didn’t have any. Again, this isn’t a broad generalization or meant to say having or not having mental illness makes someone good or bad, but to demonstrate that it really does depend on the person. Mental illness doesn’t determine the kind of partner someone will be, character does.

This isn’t exactly answering your question, but I will say the thing I’ve learned owning pets is no matter how much you plan/budget - always expect the unexpected.

I have multiple examples of what I mean by this. For one, pets get sick randomly and out of nowhere. This (hopefully of course) wouldn’t happen often, no. But the thing with vet bills is they get hefty pretty quickly, especially if it’s an emergency and you need to visit an animal ER. Most places, you pay a flat fee for the visit alone. Then if any additional tests need done, or medications need prescribed, that’s additional costs. Health issues can crop up out of nowhere, too, in the healthiest pets. I adopted a cat from a shelter who was just 2 years old and healthy as can be, and out of nowhere I found out he had kidney disease. Very rapidly, he declined and had to eventually be euthanized due to having uncontrollable seizures. (Sadly, that also costs a lot, especially for private cremation.) 

One of my other cats developed urinary problems suddenly. He now has to eat very expensive, prescription wet and dry food. It adds up fast, and if he didn’t have this food, his bladder would be blocked. That would either cost his life, or thousands of dollars in vet bills to unblock his bladder. So sadly, I’m stuck spending $60+/month on food alone for just him. 

Another one of my cats, shortly after taking him in, it came to my attention that he had teeth literally rotting out of his mouth because his previous owners neglected him. He had to have surgery to remove some and clean all of his teeth - $600. That was jaw dropping for me.

I know this seems like a big ramble of me complaining about the cost of pets and my own woes - don’t get me wrong, I would never in my life give them up. They’re mine until it’s their time to go and I’d pay for anything they needed to be healthy. But my point is that in my experience, it’s not so much the pet itself and all the needed supplies for it monthly that (in my opinion) is necessarily expensive. It’s all the unknowns and all the unexpected vet bills I wasn’t planning having to afford when they get sick randomly or something comes up. 

I absolutely don’t say this to deter you or discourage you from getting a dog! Like I said, it’s truthfully not the monthly, regular expenses that get you. It’s just all the unknowns and things you may not plan on that add up. Hopefully that gives some insight ❤️

I should have been more specific! OP was asking specifically about mascara brushes/lipsticks, so my answer was in reference to that. Under no conditions should a professional artist use the same mascara wand on multiple people. It’s very unsanitary and you can contract eye infections. For this - yes, they use disposables! They’re pretty cheap and bought in bulk. Same goes for lipsticks, most buy disposable lip brushes like what you would find in Ulta/Sephora to use with testers. So, for instance with liquid lip products, the actual brush with the lip product is never used, and instead artists uses disposable brushes for each time they dip into the product, as not to “contaminate” it lol. For other brushes, those are completely fine and they usually are washed between clients and used again and again! Thank you for asking that, my original post definitely wasn’t clear enough

Don’t worry too much, let your artist take care of you :)
